text: In Republic II, education begins with stories, since children hear them before they are trained in gymnastics (376e–377a). The founders of the city must therefore supervise the makers of stories (377b–c), and Socrates lays down two laws for what may be said about the gods. The first is that God is good, and because he is good he causes good things only. The evils in human life far outnumber the goods, and for these some other cause must be found, since nothing good can do harm (379a–c). The second law holds that God neither changes nor deceives. Whatever is in the best condition is least altered from outside, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse (380d–381c). Three kinds of story are excluded: Homer's two jars standing at the threshold of Zeus (379d), any poet who blames a god for the ruin of a household (380a), and the shape-shifting gods of the old tales (381d). Gods and human beings hate the lie in the soul most, more than the spoken lie. That lie is the condition of being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself (382a–b). A god has no such lie within him, and he has no motive to plant one in anyone else (382e).
